Macrons

Consonantal i

Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

improve verb

get better

also get better, improvement

classical

Cic. Off. 3.37 (Lewis & Short): sī modo in philosophiā aliquid prōfēcimus
Quint. 10.1.112: ille sē prōfēcisse sciat, cui Cicerō valdē placēbit
Traupman 30, 154

prōficiō, prōficere, prōfēcī, prōfectum

verb, third conjugation (-iō), intransitive

make progress, get better (at something)

Of progress in learning or a skill, often with aliquid, multum or nihil: nihil prōficere is to get nowhere. Traupman’s word for improving in one’s studies; his noun for “improvement” is prōfectus.

Other words

  • melior fierī — become better

    also used · classical · Hor. Epist. 2.2.211: lēnior et melior fīs accēdente senectā?; Traupman 154

    Of a person or a thing becoming better in any way.

  • in melius mūtārī — change for the better

    also used · classical · Sen. Ep. 47.21: saepe mūtātur, nōn in melius, sed in aliud; M-O s.v. improve

  • meliusculē esse — be a little better (after an illness)

    also used · classical · Cic. Fam. 16.5.1: cum meliusculē tibi esset

    (vōx sermōnis cotīdiānī: Plaut.; Cic. in epistulīs)

    With a dative of the person. A rare adverb: Lewis & Short cites this line of Cicero’s, Fronto, and Plautus in another sense. To recover from an illness is convalēscere (see I feel better).

Examples

  • nātālīs grātē numerās? ignōscis amīcīs? lēnior et melior fīs accēdente senectā?

    Do you count your birthdays gratefully? Do you forgive your friends? Are you growing gentler and better as old age comes on?Hor. Epist. 2.2.210–211

  • ille sē prōfēcisse sciat, cui Cicerō valdē placēbit

    Let a man know that he has made progress when Cicero delights him.Quint. 10.1.112

  • ‘quantum’ inquis ‘prōficiam?’ quantum temptāveris

    “How far will I get?” you ask. As far as you try.Sen. Ep. 76.5

See also improve, I feel better, practice, develop.
